new_statements.quote: The Kayah Li phonological word is the structure of those lexical items which are neither analyzeable compounds; truly polysyllabic morphemes ... This structure may be abbreviated as: [t T t / cv CCV v]. Upper-case elements are required, and lower-case are optional ... CCV is main syllable; post-main syllable v is a suffix. ... the pre-main syllable element symbolized cv above, which I will call presyllable (another possibility would have been the term 'minor syllable' ...). [p. 343] ... Thus presyllables are phonologically dependent on their associated main syllables [p. 344] ... In these it has only some of the phonological characteristics of a prefix: it is unstressed, at or near low-level pitch, and its vowel quality approaches [ə]. [pp. 350-351]
new_statements.citation: Solnit, David B. 1992. When is an affix not a morpheme? Minor syllables in Kayah Li. Papers from the First Annual Meeting of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society (SEALS I, 1991), 343-355.

new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (13-page SEAlang scan, pp. 343-355, no text layer) and rendered scan pages 1, 2, 8, 9 (= printed pp. 343, 344, 350, 351) at 110 dpi to read against the scanned file. All three stitched passages are on the page as quoted: p. 343 'The Kayah Li* phonological word is the structure of those lexical items which are neither analyzeable compounds; truly polysyllabic morphemes... This structure may be abbreviated as:' followed by the two-line diagram (t T t over c v C C V v; the quote linearizes it as '[t T t / cv CCV v]'), then 'Upper-case elements are required, and lower-case are optional... CCV is main syllable; post-main syllable v is a suffix. T= /á/ high, /ā/ mid, /a/ (unmarked) low-lev…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kayah Li is a tone language (four tones) with sesquisyllabic words: an optional reduced presyllable (minor syllable: C+schwa/copy vowel or ?i-, with restricted tones) precedes the full main syllable, which carries the contrastive tone and the stress; presyllables are unstressed and phonologically dependent on the following main syllable. Stress therefore falls on the (last) full/major syllable of the phonological word, i.e. a right-headed (iambic) pattern (Bennett 1995 abstract: 'consistent pattern of metrical right-headedness... iambic foot structure... major syllables and minor syllables'). Solnit 1997 p.17 / 2003 p.624 note that in disyllabic compounds such as be se 'face' the first element can be unstressed with vowel lowering (/bəse/), so the same right-headed reduction extends to compounds.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed by any opened source; Bennett 1995 abstract says Southeast Asian languages, Kayah Li included, 'lack the alternating patterns of multiple stress levels'.
new_statements.exceptions: The prefix-like ?a is only partly reduced (retains [a] and no vowel harmony at slower tempos); a rare suffix syllable (copy vowel with high-falling tone) follows the main syllable, so the stressed syllable is not always word-final; presyllable reduction is tempo/speech-style dependent (Solnit 1992 p.344, 2003 p.625; Bennett 1995).
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (lexical item): presyllable + main syllable (+ suffix); observations in isolation/citation forms and connected speech; compounds mentioned only via the be se example. The stress statement is a passing observation about presyllables, not a formulated stress rule.
new_statements.identity_note: All of Solnit's data (1992 paper, 1997 grammar, 2003 sketch) describe Eastern Kayah Li, Lower (kê kê) dialect, as spoken by refugees/settlers in Mae Hong Son province, Thailand (2003 p. 623: 'The language described in this chapter is the Lower variety'; 1992 fn.: Eastern dialect area, Mae Hong Son 1983-84, 1987-88) = east2342 [eky]. Bennett 1995 says only 'Kayah Li'; Bryant 1996 shows Bennett worked with both an Eastern (Khu Klawreh) and a Western (Khu Noah) speaker, so the dialect behind his metrical analysis is unverified (Western Kayah = kaya1317? / iso kyu, not checked). Bryant & Paulsen 1996 (examined, no stress) is Western Kayah Li [kyu], a different language.

sources.note: pp. 343-344: the phonological word is presyllable (cv, restricted C/V/T inventory) + main syllable (CCV) + optional suffix (v); presyllables are 'phonologically dependent on their associated main syllables' (tone dissimilation in ?i-, copy-vowel/schwa in Ca-); pp. 350-351: the prefix-like ?a 'has only some of the phonological characteristics of a prefix: it is unstressed, at or near low-level pitch, and its vowel quality approaches [schwa]'. No sentence stating a stress-placement rule; the unstressed status of presyllables is stated in passing. Eastern dialect data, Mae Hong Son 1983-84, 1987…

sources.note: p. 13 'Kayah Li is a tone language'; p. 17 note 3 'When unstressed, /e/ may lower. This is especially noticeable in the word /be se/ face, which often sounds more like /bese/'; p. 20 four major tones + marginal high falling (a suffix tone). p. 4: most morphemes monosyllabic, 'prefix' = CV syllable with drastically reduced segmental and tonal contrasts. The excerpt ends at 2.4 Tones; any later section on word structure/stress (2.5 ff.) is not in the excerpt.
